title: Locking GitHub Actions with workflow lockfiles
excerpt: GitHub Actions now support lockfiles to pin exact commits and prevent supply-chain attacks.
body:
A recent GitHub status incident showed how a mutable tag in an Action can cascade across many projects. An attacker retagged a previously safe version to malicious code, exposing the supply-chain risk that comes from pulling actions directly from Git. Because actions are fetched from Git, the safest practice is to lock each step to an exact commit SHA. GitHub now supports workflow lockfiles, letting a repository record those SHAs automatically and verify them in CI.

The lockfile approach removes the need to hunt down every `uses:` line and replace a tag with a SHA by hand. The `gh-actions-lock` extension generates a machine-readable file that lists every action, its version tag, and the exact commit it points to.

When the workflow runs, a verification step can fail the job if the lockfile is out of sync, preventing accidental or malicious drift. The following sections walk through installing the extension, generating a lockfile, and enforcing verification in a pipeline.

## Install the gh-actions-lock extension

The source provides the exact commands needed to add the extension to the GitHub CLI.

```bash
gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock
```

The command writes a small binary into the `gh` plugin directory and registers the `actions-lock` subcommand. Once installed, `gh actions-lock` can be run in any repository that contains a `.github/workflows` directory. The extension scans each workflow file, resolves every `uses:` reference to the commit SHA that the tag currently points at, and writes the results to `.github/workflows/actions.lock`.

## Generate and commit a lockfile

Running `gh actions-lock` creates the lockfile and updates the workflow files to use stable tags instead of raw SHAs. In the example from the source, the `actions/checkout` step changes from:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1 # v7.0.1
```

to the cleaner tag form:

```yaml
- uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
```

The lockfile records the underlying SHA (`sha1-3d3c42e5aac5ba805825da76410c181273ba90b1`) so that later verification can compare the current tag resolution against the saved value. The same transformation happens for the `j178/prek-action` step, which moves from a full SHA to `j178/prek-action@v3.1.0`.

After generation, add the lockfile to version control alongside the workflow files. A typical commit message might read “Add actions.lock generated by gh-actions-lock”. Because the lockfile is deterministic, subsequent runs will produce the same file as long as the workflow definitions have not changed. Editing a workflow, adding a new action, or changing a version will cause the lockfile to diverge, and the verification step will catch the mismatch.

## Verify lockfiles in CI

GitHub recommends a verification job that runs on every push, pull request, or manual dispatch. The source provides a minimal job definition that can be dropped into an existing workflow or placed in a dedicated `verify-lockfile.yml`.

```yaml
lockfile:
  runs-on: ubuntu-slim
  env:
    GH_TOKEN: ${{ github.token }}
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v7.0.1
      with:
        persist-credentials: false
    - run: gh extension install github/gh-actions-lock --pin v0.4.1
    - run: gh actions-lock --verify
```

The job runs on an `ubuntu-slim` runner, installs the extension (pinning to a known version, e.g., `v0.4.1`), and executes `gh actions-lock --verify`. If the lockfile does not match the current workflow definitions or if any pinned action fails to resolve to the recorded commit, the step exits with a non-zero status and the job fails.

The verification step uses the `GH_TOKEN` secret automatically provided by GitHub Actions, so it can read private repositories if needed. The source notes that the lockfile verification also catches “a locked pin no longer verifies upstream”, covering cases where a tag is retagged after the lockfile was created. This protects against the supply-chain attack scenario described at the start of the post.

Because the lockfile lives in the repository, any developer who forgets to run `gh actions-lock` after editing a workflow will see the CI job fail. The failure message points directly to the out-of-date lockfile, making remediation straightforward: run `gh actions-lock` locally, commit the updated `actions.lock`, and push again.

## The takeaway

Locking GitHub Actions with a workflow lockfile records exact commit SHAs for every step and lets CI verify that the file stays in sync. Install the `gh-actions-lock` extension, generate and commit the lockfile, and add a verification job to each workflow. This small addition prevents mutable tags from drifting and guards the supply chain against accidental or malicious changes.  

*Source: [Lock Your GitHub Actions](https://hugovk.dev/blog/2026/lock-github-actions/); [GitHub Incident with Webhooks, Actions, etc.](https://www.githubstatus.com/incidents/dvy0t3mvh1lg)*
